t: Entering Academic Writing in a Korean University
x: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Identify the purposes and conventions of academic writing. Distinguish analytical, persuasive, descriptive, and critical functions. Create a personal plan for entering an unfamiliar academic discourse community. Learning objectives academic discourse evidence claim register scholarly identity audience Key terms Academic writing is not simply formal English. It is a disciplined way of making knowledge visible to a particular community. A successful text states a purpose, develops claims through reasons and evidence, acknowledges sources, and guides readers through a transparent structure. At a Korean university, international students may encounter conventions that differ from those at their previous schools. The appropriate response is not to abandon prior knowledge, but to learn how expectations are expressed in the present department, course, and assignment. Academic writing as situated communication Effective academic prose is clear, precise, evidence-based, ethically sourced, and logically organized. Formality does not require inflated vocabulary or constant passive voice. Writers should select active or passive constructions according to emphasis, define technical terms, quantify claims when the evidence permits, and avoid presenting interpretations as facts. Every paragraph should perform an identifiable function in the larger argument. Core qualities A single paper commonly combines several functions. Description establishes what was observed; analysis explains patterns and relationships; persuasion advances a defensible position; and critical writing evaluates assumptions, methods, or implications. International students should identify the function required at each point rather than assuming that all academic writing must sound equally abstract. Writing functions Assignment sheets, journal articles recommended by the instructor, departmental thesis templates, and professors' feedback are evidence of local conventions. When expectations remain implicit, ask focused questions: What kind of claim is expected? Which citation system applies? How much methodological detail is required? A precise question demonstrates preparation and reduces the risk of misunderstanding. Learning local expectations Academic writing is socially situated: readers judge a text against the purposes, evidence practices, and genre conventions of a particular community. International students in Korea therefore need two forms of knowledge simultaneously. They need broadly transferable principles—clear claims, warranted evidence, transparent source use, and coherent organization—and local knowledge about how a department interprets those principles. A course paper, capstone report, laboratory report, thesis proposal, and journal manuscript may all be described as "academic writing." Yet, each assigns different weight to originality, replication, critical synthesis, and practical contribution. At the beginning of an assignment, convert tacit expectations into written questions. Ask what document type is required, who will evaluate it, which language and citation style are expected, whether Korean-language evidence is acceptable, and what counts as an original contribution at the relevant level. At a Korean university, the answer may be distributed across the syllabus, departmental regulations, a graduate school handbook, a laboratory convention, and an instructor's oral guidance. Record the answer and the source of the instruction. When two instructions conflict, seek clarification before drafting, not after submission. Academic English should not require erasing a multilingual identity. Multilingual writers can plan, search, annotate, and test ideas across languages, provided that the final English text explains culturally or institutionally specific concepts and maintains stable terminology. Translanguaging can function as a resource for knowledge construction, but the published argument must remain accessible to its intended readers (Canagarajah, 2013). By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Differentiate quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods approaches. Align a research question with an appropriate form of evidence. Recognize standards for data quality and credible interpretation. Learning objectives quantitative research qualitative research mixed methods data validity reliability trustworthiness triangulation Key terms Research is a systematic response to a meaningful question. Although the source text emphasizes education, the underlying logic applies across disciplines: define a problem, determine what evidence could answer it, collect and analyze that evidence rigorously, and explain the limits of the resulting claim. Disciplinary differences affect what counts as data, which methods are legitimate, and how findings are reported. Research as systematic inquiry Quantitative research examines variables through numerical data and statistical analysis. Qualitative research investigates experience, meaning, practice, or context through materials such as interviews, observations, documents, or artifacts. Mixed-methods research combines quantitative and qualitative components when their integration offers a stronger response than either component alone. The label should follow the research purpose, not fashion. Three broad approaches A question about prevalence may require a survey or dataset; a question about lived experience may require interviews; a question about change may require longitudinal, experimental, design-based, or comparative evidence. Researchers must also consider access, sampling, measurement, language, time, and ethics. Pilot testing can reveal unclear questions or impractical procedures before full data collection begins. From question to evidence Data do not explain themselves. Quantitative analysis requires appropriate statistical procedures and cautious interpretation of association and causation. Qualitative analysis requires an explicit analytic process and evidence that interpretations are grounded in the data. Validity and reliability are common quantitative concerns; qualitative researchers often discuss credibility, dependability, confirmability, and transferability. Triangulation may strengthen an interpretation when multiple sources genuinely address the same question. Credible analysis and interpretation Research quality cannot be reduced to one universal method. Engineering may prioritize performance under specified conditions; natural sciences may foreground measurement and reproducibility; health research may require participant protection and protocol transparency; humanities research may build an interpretive claim from texts, artifacts, or archives. The common principle is alignment: the question determines what evidence is relevant, and the claims must not exceed what the design and data can support. Before collecting data, identify the reporting standard used by the relevant field. Reporting guidelines do not replace methodological judgment, but they provide information readers need to evaluate a study. The EQUATOR Network organizes designspecific guidance, including CONSORT for randomized trials, STROBE for observational studies, and COREQ for qualitative interviews and focus groups (EQUATOR Network, 2026). The updated CONSORT 2025 statement emphasizes complete and transparent reporting of randomized trials (CONSORT Group, 2025). Students in other fields should identify an equivalent disciplinary standard or the author instructions of a respected journal. Use a design memo with five columns: research question, evidence needed, source or participant, analytic procedure, and permitted claim. This memo is especially valuable when a project combines methods. Mixed-methods research is not made coherent by collecting numbers and interviews; the researcher must explain why integration is needed, where it occurs, and what inference becomes possible because of it. Cross-disciplinary evidence and reporting standards A chemistry student reporting a synthesis should preserve reagent specifications, instrument settings, calibration information, exclusions, and unsuccessful conditions when these affect interpretation. Reproducibility begins with records detailed enough for another qualified researcher to understand what was done. Discipline rotation—natural sciences Question-method mismatch Better alignment How do first-year international students Use interviews or focus groups for experience group work? A closed yes/no detailed accounts, and add a survey only if survey alone is unlikely to capture the the study also needs evidence about process or meaning of that experience. broader patterns. Graduate application: Draft a question-evidence-method alignment table for your proposed thesis or article. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Explain how writing supports research decisions. Use structure to make complex reasoning traceable. Treat drafting as part of inquiry rather than as final transcription. Learning objectives research argument coherence transparency reproducibility knowledge dissemination Key terms Writing does more than report a completed study. It reveals gaps in reasoning, forces definitions, and makes the relationship among a problem, evidence, and conclusion inspectable. A researcher who cannot explain why a method answers a question may not yet have achieved adequate alignment. Drafting early therefore improves both the project and the final paper. Writing is part of research The familiar sequence of introduction, literature review, methodology, findings or results, discussion, and conclusion represents a chain of reasoning. The introduction establishes the problem; the literature review situates it within the knowledge; the methodology justifies the inquiry; the findings present the analysis; and the discussion explains what the findings mean. Not every discipline uses identical labels, but readers still need this logical progression. Structure as a research tool Complexity should be organized, not erased. Define the unit of analysis, specify scope, separate observation from interpretation, and signal relationships among ideas. Headings, topic sentences, tables, and figures should help readers understand the argument rather than decorate the document. Precise writing also makes a study easier to evaluate and, where applicable, reproduce. Clarity without oversimplification For international students, academic writing is also a means of joining a scholarly community. Participation requires more than grammatical accuracy: it involves citing others fairly, making a contribution proportional to the evidence, responding to feedback, and recognizing how disciplinary and institutional conventions shape communication. Writing for participation Research writing is not an ornamental stage added after analysis. A precise methods section exposes design weaknesses; a results section tests whether the analysis actually answers the questions; and a discussion reveals whether interpretation has outrun the evidence. Drafting should therefore begin with provisional claims, evidence maps, and decision logs while the project is still developing. Maintain three linked records: a research log that documents procedural decisions, a source matrix that records how each source is used, and a claim-evidence table that connects every major assertion to data or scholarship. These records reduce accidental misrepresentation and make revision more efficient. They also support responsible collaboration because contributors can see how a conclusion developed. When writing with digital or AI-supported tools, preserve human accountability. UNESCO's guidance recommends a human-centered approach that attends to privacy, validation, equity, and the limits of generated content (Miao & Holmes, 2023). Never enter confidential participant data, unpublished proprietary material, or identifiable student information into an unapproved system. Verify every generated factual statement and citation against the source. Writing as a reproducible record of reasoning Untraceable claim Traceable claim The method was Semi-structured interviews were appropriate because the appropriate, and the study examined how participants interpreted a shared results were institutional experience; the recurring accounts support a meaningful. contextual, rather than universal, conclusion. Worked revision Undergraduate application Create a one-page map showing how the sections of a research report answer different reader questions. Graduate application Write a 200-word alignment statement connecting your problem, question, evidence, and intended contribution. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Translate a research idea into manageable stages. Identify dependencies, resources, and risks. Use milestones to manage an undergraduate or graduate project. Learning objectives scope feasibility milestone dependency research log data management Key terms A research project usually moves through problem identification, preliminary reading, question development, design, ethical review where required, data collection, analysis, drafting, revision, and dissemination. The process is iterative: reading may refine a question, pilot data may change an instrument, and analysis may expose the need for a clearer conceptual definition. The research cycle A valuable question must also be answerable with the available time, access, knowledge, language resources, and data. Narrowing a project is not intellectual failure. It is a methodological decision that allows the writer to make a defensible claim. International students should account for unfamiliar administrative processes, translation needs, and time for communication when estimating a schedule. Feasibility before ambition Convert the research cycle into dated outputs: a one-page problem statement, an annotated source set, a question-method matrix, an ethics submission, a cleaned dataset, an analysis memo, and section drafts. Record decisions and file versions. A research log should state what changed, why it changed, and what evidence supported the change. Project management Common risks include delayed participant access, unusable data, overly broad questions, unclear authorship roles, and late discovery of formatting requirements. Identify a mitigation strategy for each major risk. For example, confirm data access before committing to a study design, and obtain the official thesis template before formatting the final document. Managing risk A workable project plan begins with institutional deadlines and moves backward. For a thesis, map proposal approval, ethics review when applicable, recruitment or data access, analysis, committee review, similarity checking, formatting review, defense, corrections, and repository submission. Names and sequences vary by university and department; verify them in the current graduate-school and departmental rules rather than relying on another student's memory. Create two schedules. The compliance schedule contains fixed external dates and required approvals. The research schedule contains adjustable work packages, dependencies, buffers, and decision points. Do not schedule data collection before any required ethics approval or permission. Do not assume that a supervisor can review a full thesis immediately before an administrative deadline. Send a realistic review request that identifies the document, its stage, the type of feedback needed, and the date by which feedback would remain useful. Risk planning is not pessimism. Record at least one alternative for recruitment failure, delayed equipment, restricted database access, transcription volume, software incompatibility, and nonresponse from a partner organization. A smaller, more complete study is usually stronger than an ambitious project that cannot adequately document or analyze its evidence. Korean universities. Worked revision Undergraduate application: Build an eight-week schedule for a course research paper, including two revision points. Graduate application: Create a thesis milestone plan that includes ethics, recruitment, data management, analysis, committee feedback, and submission. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Apply principles of consent, privacy, and responsible authorship. Distinguish quotation, paraphrase, summary, and plagiarism. Recognize when institutional approval is required. Learning objectives informed consent confidentiality anonymity plagiarism authorship conflict of interest institutional review Key terms Ethics is not a form completed after a design has been finalized. It shapes the research question, recruitment, consent, data handling, analysis, representation, authorship, and dissemination. Researchers should minimize harm, communicate honestly, respect participants, and avoid claims that exceed the evidence. Ethics throughout the project Requirements vary by institution and discipline. Before collecting data from people or using protected records, consult the responsible professor, department, and institutional review process. Do not assume that classroom access, workplace access, or possession of data constitutes permission to use those materials for research. Institutional requirements in Korea A quotation reproduces exact language and requires quotation marks or block formatting plus a citation. A paraphrase expresses the source's meaning in a genuinely new structure and wording while retaining a citation. A summary condenses a larger argument and also requires attribution. Changing a few words is not an adequate paraphrase. Maintain notes that clearly separate copied language from your own writing. Source use and plagiarism Discuss contribution, authorship order, file ownership, and decision authority early. Keep a record of contributions and disclose conflicts of interest. Translation, language editing, statistical support, and generative tools should be used only in accordance with applicable course, journal, and institutional rules. The named author remains accountable for accuracy and integrity. Responsible collaboration Ethics review and research integrity are related but not identical. Research involving people, identifiable private information, or human-derived materials may require review by an Institutional Review Board (IRB; 기관생명윤리위원회) before data collection. Korea's institutional system operates under the Bioethics and Safety Act, and the National Institute for Bioethics Policy provides information and shared-review services (National Institute for Bioethics Policy, 2026). Students must use their own institution's current procedures and must not describe a project as "exempt" unless the authorized process has made that determination. Research integrity also governs projects that do not require IRB review. It includes honest data handling, accurate reporting, traceable source use, disclosure of conflicts of interest, appropriate credit, and correction of errors. The Korean Ministry of Education's researchethics guidance applies institutional responsibilities and misconduct procedures broadly to research outputs, including theses and academic articles (Ministry of Education, 2022). Keep raw data, processed data, code, consent records, and analytic decisions in approved locations for the period required by the institution or funder. Discuss authorship early and revisit it when roles change. Contribution, accountability, and approval—not status alone—should determine authorship. Use a written contribution table covering conceptualization, methodology, data work, analysis, software, visualization, drafting, and revision. The CRediT taxonomy supplies a standardized vocabulary for describing contributor roles (National Information Standards Organization [NISO], 2022). The order of authors differs across fields, so supervisors and students should explicitly agree on the intended convention, the corresponding author, revision duties, and the conditions under which the order may change. A generative-AI system cannot accept responsibility for a paper and should not be listed as an author. If a tool is permitted, document its name and version, purpose, material supplied to it, verification performed, and any disclosure required by the course, university, journal, or research team. Human authors remain accountable for accuracy, originality, confidentiality, bias, and citations (Miao & Holmes, 2023). Research integrity, IRB review, authorship, and generative AI A public-health student interviewing patients must address recruitment power dynamics, informed consent, privacy, distress, secure storage, and the consequences of quoting potentially identifiable narratives. Scientific value does not cancel the obligation to protect participants. Graduate application Draft a data protection and authorship agreement for a collaborative research project. x: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Analyze audience, genre, and assessment expectations. Establish a sustainable writing environment. Use multilingual resources without weakening authorial responsibility. Learning objectives genre rhetorical purpose assignment brief academic register multilingual writer Key terms Identify the required genre, purpose, audience, length, evidence, citation style, and submission format. Terms such as discuss, evaluate, compare, and critically analyze signal different intellectual operations. If a prompt remains ambiguous, provide an interpretation and ask a focused question rather than asking the instructor to restate the entire assignment. Read the task before writing A model text should be analyzed for moves, not copied for sentences. Observe how the writer introduces the problem, positions sources, qualifies claims, organizes evidence, and concludes. Select models from the relevant discipline and genre because conventions differ across laboratory reports, humanities essays, design projects, and social-science theses. Develop a multilingual workflow. Thinking, note-taking, and planning may occur in more than one language. This can expand conceptual resources, but the final argument must remain coherent in English. Define Korean institutional terms when a direct English equivalent is misleading. Keep terminology consistent and avoid literal translation of expressions whose rhetorical force changes across languages. Study models strategically Writing improves through repeated sessions. Set a specific output for each session, remove avoidable distractions, and separate drafting from final editing. Use feedback and tools to diagnose problems, but verify every change. A fluent sentence is not necessarily an accurate sentence. Create workable conditions International students often search and think across languages. Use this capacity deliberately. Maintain a bilingual term bank containing the Korean term, preferred English rendering, definition, source, and notes on context. Examples include 학위논문 (thesis or dissertation, depending on the degree and institutional usage), 논문계획서 (thesis or research proposal), 예비심사 (preliminary review), 본심사 (final examination or final review), 수정대조표 (revision response table), and 지도교수 (academic advisor, research supervisor, or thesis supervisor). Choose the English term that accurately describes the function; do not assume a one-to-one translation. When citing a Korean source in an English paper, preserve retrievability. Romanize the author's name consistently, translate the title when required by the citation style, identify the original language if useful, and retain the original journal or publisher information accurately. A translation of a quotation is still a quotation: cite the source and indicate that the translation is yours unless an official translation is used. For a paraphrase, verify meaning against the Korean original rather than paraphrasing an automated English translation alone. English names, institutional affiliations, addresses, and degree names should follow official sources. Use the spelling found in the student information system or passport when required; use the university's official English name; and copy the formal English degree title from the university's regulations or diploma documentation. Consistency across the manuscript, submission system, ethics application, and publication metadata prevents indexing and identity problems. May I organize the body by evaluation paper. criterion rather than discussing each theory separately? By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Use recursive planning and drafting strategies. Build paragraphs around claims and evidence. Revise at global, paragraph, and sentence levels. Learning objectives outline reverse outline topic sentence cohesion coherence revision Key terms Begin with a working question and a provisional answer. Group evidence by the reasons that support that answer, not merely by the order in which sources were read. An outline should display relationships among claims. It may change as the writer discovers new evidence or identifies a stronger structure. Plan the argument A paragraph should advance one controlling idea. The topic sentence establishes its function; evidence supports the point; analysis explains how the evidence matters; and a transition connects the paragraph to the larger argument. Paragraph length should follow the work required, not a fixed number of sentences. Draft functional paragraphs Global revision addresses purpose, argument, evidence, and organization. Paragraph revision addresses unity, development, and progression. Sentence editing addresses clarity, precision, grammar, and style. Proofreading comes last. Correcting commas in a section that will later be deleted wastes time. Revise in layers Do not treat feedback as a list of corrections. Categorize comments, identify recurring causes, and decide what revision principle applies across the text. When advice conflicts, return to the assignment, evidence, and decision authority. Keep a revision memo that records substantial changes. Use feedback actively Effective feedback begins with a focused request. Sending an entire draft with "Please check my English" transfers an undefined task to the reader. Instead, identify the document stage and two or three priorities: argument structure, methodological alignment, interpretation, or sentence-level editing. If the draft is incomplete, label missing sections and state what kind of response would help at that stage. A respectful academic email in Korea should be concise and explicit. Use a subject line that names the course or project and action, address the instructor with the appropriate title, give necessary context, state the request, propose a realistic date, and attach a clearly named file. Example: "Subject: Request for feedback on thesis proposal methods section—Kim, Applied Linguistics. Dear Professor Park, I have revised the sampling and analysis sections following our July 10 meeting. Could you please comment on whether the proposed analysis answers Research Question 2? Feedback by July 24 would allow me to revise before the departmental deadline on August 2. The revised file and a one-page change summary are attached." After a meeting, send a short decision record when the project is complex: what was agreed, what you will do, what the supervisor will review, and the next date. This is not a legalistic record; it prevents language-related misunderstandings and makes progress visible. In laboratories and seminars, observe local norms about circulation, response time, speaking order, and credit, but request clarification when a norm affects authorship, ethics, safety, or assessment. Feedback cycles with instructors and supervisors Evidence without analysis Synthesis Across the studies, difficulties arose not from Several studies reported language alone but from the interaction of difficulties. Kim (2021) found X. language, institutional access, and disciplinary Lee (2020) found Y. expectations. Worked revision Undergraduate application: Reverse-outline a completed draft by writing the function of each paragraph in the margin. Graduate application: Prepare a revision memo that prioritizes three global changes before sentence editing. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Move from a topic to a researchable problem. Establish context, significance, and a knowledge gap. Write aligned purposes and research questions. Learning objectives topic problem knowledge gap purpose statement research question significance Key terms A topic names an area; a problem identifies a condition that requires explanation or response; a knowledge gap identifies what existing scholarship has not adequately established. A gap is not merely the absence of a study in one location. The writer must explain why the missing knowledge matters and how the proposed inquiry can address it. Topic, problem, and gap Begin with the broader context, narrow to a specific condition, synthesize what is known, identify a limitation or unresolved issue, and state the consequence of leaving it unresolved. Then state the study's purpose. This sequence allows readers to understand why the project is necessary before encountering detailed questions or methods. Problem-building sequence Questions should be specific, answerable, ethically appropriate, and consistent with the intended evidence. Avoid combining several studies into one question. Terms such as impact or effect may imply a causal design; use them only when the design can support causal inference. Qualitative questions often emphasize how, what, or in what ways. Aligned research questions Significance may be conceptual, methodological, practical, or contextual. State the likely contribution at the scale supported by the project. An undergraduate study may clarify a local pattern; a graduate study may refine a concept or provide evidence for a disciplinary debate. Neither should promise to solve a national problem without adequate evidence. Significance without exaggeration A research problem is not established merely because an issue matters. The writer must show what is known, what remains uncertain or contested, why the uncertainty matters to a defined audience, and how the proposed study can produce relevant evidence. Avoid turning personal difficulties into universal claims about all international students or all Korean universities. Use a four-part problem statement: context, established knowledge, bounded gap, and consequence. Then align each research question with a feasible unit of analysis and evidence source. A question about experience may require interviews or reflective records; a performance question may require a defined outcome measure; a question about institutional policy may require document analysis and stakeholder perspectives. Local relevance and wider contribution can coexist. A single Korean university may be a theoretically informative case if the boundaries and selection logic are explicit. The researcher should not claim national representativeness unless the sampling and design support it. State what the study can illuminate, not what it cannot prove. t: Building a Conceptual or Theoretical Foundation
x: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Distinguish theory, theoretical framework, and conceptual framework. Select a framework for analytical usefulness. Integrate a framework throughout a study. Learning objectives theory concept theoretical framework conceptual framework analytical lens Key terms A framework identifies concepts and relationships that guide attention. It can shape the research question, definitions, data collection, analysis, and interpretation. A theory should not appear only in the literature review; if it matters to the study, readers should be able to see how it influenced methodological and analytical decisions. What a framework does A theoretical framework applies or combines established theory to interpret a problem. A conceptual framework may assemble concepts from research and practice into a studyspecific model. Terminology varies by discipline, so writers should follow local conventions and define how the term is being used. Theoretical and conceptual frameworks Choose a framework because it clarifies the research problem and supports analysis, not because it is popular. Examine its assumptions, unit of analysis, prior applications, and limits. A framework developed in another context may still be useful, but the writer should justify its transfer and avoid treating it as culturally universal. Selecting a framework Introduce the framework, define its central concepts, explain relevant relationships, review how it has been used, justify its fit, and state exactly how it will guide the present study. A diagram may help when it communicates relationships more efficiently than prose, but every element must also be explained in the text. Writing the foundation A framework identifies what the researcher will attend to and how concepts are related; it does not guarantee a result. Explain the framework's origin, central constructs, assumptions, and relevance to the problem. Then show how it informs research questions, sampling, instruments, coding, or interpretation. If it affects none of these decisions, it may be decorative rather than functional. International students should be cautious when transferring a framework developed in another national or disciplinary context. Do not reject it merely because it is foreign, but examine whether its constructs, categories, and presumed relationships fit the Korean setting. Define local institutional features that may modify the framework, and distinguish adaptation from confirmation. In interdisciplinary work, a conceptual framework may integrate several bodies of scholarship. Make the integration visible through a diagram or proposition set, and define the level at which each concept operates. Avoid combining theories only because they share a keyword. Using theory without forcing the data A human–computer interaction study may combine a usability construct with cognitiveload theory. The framework should specify which measures represent each construct and how design features are expected to influence performance or user experience. t: Conducting and Writing a Literature Review
x: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Search, evaluate, organize, and synthesize literature. Differentiate a source list from a literature review. Use citations to construct a scholarly position. Learning objectives search strategy inclusion criteria synthesis research gap citation chaining literature matrix Key terms A literature review explains what a field knows, how it knows it, where findings converge or conflict, and what remains unresolved. It should establish the intellectual context for the present project. A sequence of article summaries does not accomplish this purpose because it leaves relationships among sources implicit. Purpose of the review Translate the research problem into concepts and search terms, including relevant synonyms. Search appropriate databases, follow reference lists, and examine later works that cite influential studies. Record databases, terms, dates, and inclusion decisions so the search can be explained and updated. Language and database access may shape what becomes visible; acknowledge those limits. Search transparently Assess relevance, methodological quality, context, and contribution rather than relying on publication prestige alone. A literature matrix can record purpose, theory, method, sample or materials, findings, limitations, and relevance. Organize the review by themes, debates, methods, chronology, or conceptual relationships, as appropriate to the argument. Evaluate and organize Synthesis places multiple sources in relation to one another. Use citations to support a claim about the literature, then explain patterns, contradictions, or limitations. Distinguish the cited authors' conclusions from your evaluation. Conclude by showing how the review leads to the present question and contribution. Synthesize Choose a review type according to the question. A narrative review can interpret and connect a body of scholarship, but it should still explain the scope and selection. A systematic review uses prespecified, reproducible methods to answer a focused question. A scoping review maps concepts, evidence types, and gaps in a field when it is broad or heterogeneous. PRISMA 2020 provides a reporting framework for systematic reviews, while the PRISMA-ScR extension addresses scoping reviews (Page et al., 2021; Tricco et al., 2018). For Korean and international literature, search across multiple ecosystems when the topic warrants it. RISS International indexes Korean journal articles, theses, books, and serials and supports searches in Korean or English (Korea Education and Research Information Service [KERIS], 2026). Pair it with discipline-appropriate international databases, and record the database, platform, date, complete search string, filters, and result count for each. Search Korean synonyms, romanized variants, and official English institutional terms. A literature review must synthesize rather than inventory. Organize evidence by problem, concept, method, result pattern, or debate—not by a sequence of article summaries. Use a synthesis matrix to compare population, setting, design, evidence, limitations, and relevance. Cite the primary source for a substantive claim whenever possible. t: Writing Methodology as a Coherent Argument
x: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Distinguish methodology from methods. Connect philosophical assumptions, design, and procedures. Write a transparent methodology section. Learning objectives ontology epistemology paradigm methodology method positionality reflexivity Key terms Methods are procedures for generating and analyzing evidence; methodology is the reasoned approach that connects assumptions, research aims, design, and methods. Selecting an interview, survey, or statistical test without explaining this connection reduces methodology to technique. Methodology is more than tools Ontology concerns assumptions about reality; epistemology concerns what can be known and how knowledge is produced. Positivist, post-positivist, interpretive, constructivist, critical, and pragmatic traditions make different assumptions and therefore support different forms of inquiry. Writers should explain assumptions only to the depth required by the discipline and design. Philosophical assumptions A methodology section should show why the design can answer the question, how participants or materials were selected, how data were generated and analyzed, how quality was addressed, and what ethical safeguards were used. Qualitative studies may also require attention to researcher positionality and reflexivity; quantitative studies may require operational definitions, instrumentation, sampling logic, and analytical assumptions. Alignment Use causal language only when warranted. Explain limitations without undermining the entire project. Methodological transparency allows readers to evaluate what the evidence supports. The objective is not to portray the design as perfect, but to demonstrate informed, coherent, and ethical decision-making. Cautious methodological claims A methodology section is an argument that the selected design can answer the research questions ethically and credibly. It should identify the research setting, unit of analysis, participants or materials, selection logic, instruments or procedures, analytic process, quality safeguards, and limitations. Report decisions with enough precision for readers to understand what occurred; do not hide uncertainty behind technical vocabulary. Quantitative reports should define variables, measurement quality, sampling, missingdata treatment, assumption checks, model specification, effect estimates, uncertainty intervals, and any deviations from the plan. Qualitative reports should explain researcher positioning, access, sampling, data generation, analytic development, reflexivity, and the evidentiary path from data to themes or interpretations. Mixed-methods reports should specify timing, priority, points of integration, and the nature of the combined inference. Preregistration, registered reports, codebooks, analysis scripts, and data-management plans can strengthen transparency when appropriate. Open science does not mean releasing protected or proprietary data. The UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science explicitly combines openness with legal, ethical, cultural, security, and privacy constraints (UNESCO, 2021). State what can be shared, with whom, under what conditions, and why any restriction is necessary. Methodological transparency across designs Tool-centered justification Methodological justification A cross-sectional survey was selected because the study sought comparable self-reports across a A survey was used because defined population; this design estimates patterns of surveys are efficient. association but does not establish temporal or causal relationships. Worked revision Undergraduate application: Explain the difference between methodology and method through an example from your field. Graduate application: Write a methodology alignment statement covering assumptions, design, sampling, data, analysis, quality, and ethics. Organize results around research questions. Integrate prose, tables, figures, and evidence. Separate presentation from interpretation when the genre requires it. Learning objectives result finding theme statistical evidence excerpt table figure Key terms The findings or results section should make the answer to each research question easy to locate. Organize by question, hypothesis, analytical category, theme, or a justified sequence. Do not reproduce the chronology of analysis unless that chronology itself matters. Answer the questions Name the analysis, identify the variables and sample, report the relevant values consistently, and describe the direction and magnitude of the pattern. Avoid interpreting statistical significance as practical importance or causation. Tables should reduce repetition; the prose should direct readers to the important pattern rather than restating every cell. Quantitative results Present themes or analytical claims and support them with carefully selected evidence. Participant excerpts should illustrate the analysis, not replace it. Provide enough context to interpret an excerpt while protecting identity. Explain variation and negative cases when they affect the claim. Qualitative findings Every table and figure needs a number, an informative title, clear labels, and a reference in the prose. Define abbreviations and provide a source note when required. A visual should answer a reader question more efficiently than prose; decorative or redundant visuals should be removed. Visual evidence The results section should answer the research questions in a planned order and separate observation from interpretation to the degree expected in the field. Report negative, null, contradictory, and incomplete findings when they affect the inference. Selective reporting weakens the trustworthiness of the entire study. Tables and figures should be understandable without duplicating the prose. Use titles that identify the content, define abbreviations, report units, and explain denominators or missing values. Do not use a graph to exaggerate a small difference through a misleading scale. For qualitative findings, provide sufficient contextualized evidence to demonstrate how the interpretation was grounded while protecting participants' identities. Before finalizing, reconcile every number, label, category, sample size, and research question across the abstract, methods, results, tables, figures, and appendices. Automated calculations and visualization tools can reduce manual errors, but the author must verify the input data, the transformations, and the outputs. Interpret findings in relation to questions and literature. State implications and limitations proportionally. Write a conclusion that closes the argument without overclaiming. Learning objectives interpretation implication limitation contribution transferability generalizability Key terms The discussion explains what the findings mean, why they may have occurred, how they relate to previous scholarship, and what they contribute. Begin with the principal answer rather than repeating the entire results section. Distinguish explanations supported by evidence from plausible alternatives. Return to the literature and framework. Identify where findings support, extend, complicate, or contradict prior work. Use the theoretical or conceptual framework as an analytical resource, not a vocabulary list. A surprising result is not automatically a contribution; explain its significance and consider methodological or contextual explanations. From result to meaning Implications should identify who could reasonably act on the findings and under what conditions. Limitations define the boundaries of interpretation. Sample, setting, measurement, language, positionality, and design may all matter. A limitation does not require apology; it requires an account of how readers should calibrate the claim. Implications and limitations A conclusion should synthesize the problem, approach, principal finding, and contribution. It may identify a focused direction for future work. Avoid introducing new evidence, making universal claims, or ending with a generic statement about the importance of research. Concluding with proportion A strong discussion begins with the most defensible answer to each research question, then explains how the results relate to prior scholarship and the conceptual framework. It distinguishes findings from possible explanations and identifies alternative interpretations. The conclusion should not introduce a new evidentiary claim. Calibrate transfer claims to the design. Statistical generalization, analytic generalization, theoretical transfer, and practical relevance are different. A small qualitative study may illuminate a mechanism or provide transferable insight without estimating prevalence. A controlled experiment may estimate an effect under specified conditions without establishing success in implementing it across every Korean university. Limitations should explain consequences, not merely list weaknesses. State which inference is restricted, whether the limitation likely changes magnitude, direction, credibility, or transferability, and what evidence would reduce the uncertainty. Avoid the ritual claim that "more research is needed"; specify the next design, comparison, population, or dataset. Discussion, transfer, and responsible limitation Overclaim Proportional conclusion Within the studied program, orientation was This study proves that associated with clearer knowledge of advising routes; orientation programs solve longitudinal research is needed to determine international students' whether this knowledge improves later academic academic problems. outcomes. Check alignment, integrity, and consistency. Separate substantive revision from proofreading. Learning objectives manuscript audit alignment consistency reference check quality assurance Key terms Confirm that the title, abstract, problem, questions, methodology, findings, discussion, and conclusion describe the same study. Track each research question through the document. Remove claims that lack evidence and evidence that does not serve the argument. Audit the argument Check that every in-text citation has a corresponding reference and every reference is cited. Verify quotations against the source, preserve page numbers where required, and confirm that paraphrases do not distort meaning. Review permissions, anonymity, authorship, acknowledgments, and disclosures. Audit sources and integrity Use one term for one concept unless a distinction is intentional. Define abbreviations once, maintain tense patterns appropriate to each section, and check tables and figures against the prose. For multilingual content, verify names, transliterations, translations, and Korean institutional terms. Audit language and terminology Apply the required template and citation style. Inspect headings, numbering, captions, margins, page breaks, table continuation, reference formatting, and accessibility. Run automated checks, but read the rendered document because software may miss clipped text, broken fields, or misleading layout. Audit the document Conduct four separate reviews. The argument audit checks alignment among problem, questions, framework, methods, results, and conclusion. The evidence audit checks every factual claim, quotation, paraphrase, table, and reference. The language audit checks terminology, stance, cohesion, names, translations, and disciplinary usage. The production audit checks headings, numbering, captions, cross-references, margins, accessibility, and submission requirements. Build a citation ledger with one row per in-text citation and columns for source file, page or location, claim supported, quotation status, and reference-list match. Select an appropriate dissemination channel. Adapt a thesis for a new audience and genre. Communicate ethically with journals, conferences, and public audiences. Learning objectives dissemination journal article conference proposal knowledge mobilization audience adaptation Key terms A thesis is not automatically a journal article, conference presentation, policy brief, or public explanation. Each genre has a different audience, length, selection process, and purpose. Rewriting requires selecting a central contribution and restructuring the material to meet the needs of the new audience. Dissemination as adaptation Consider disciplinary fit, audience, review process, access, timing, cost, and credibility. Examine a journal's aims, recent articles, and author guidance before submission. For conferences, determine whether the format is a paper, poster, panel, workshop, or short presentation. Avoid venues that promise publication without credible review or transparent practices. Choosing a channel Submission letters and inquiries should be concise and specific. Follow stated procedures, disclose related submissions, and respond to review comments respectfully. Rejection is common and should lead to a reasoned decision: revise for the same venue if invited, adapt for another venue, or reconsider the paper's central contribution. Professional communication Research may also reach practitioners, communities, policymakers, or the public. Translate technical language without changing the claim. Explain uncertainty and limitations. When participants or communities contribute knowledge, consider how findings can be returned in an accessible and respectful way. Broader audiences Transforming a thesis into an article requires a new argument for a defined journal audience. Select one contribution, reduce background that does not serve it, reanalyze when necessary, and follow the target journal's current instructions. Confirm scope, article type, word limit, data policy, ethics statements, authorship expectations, and permitted use of AI tools before submission. Treat peer review as structured argument testing. Create a response table with the reviewer comment, the action taken, the manuscript location, and the reason when a suggestion is not adopted. Respond respectfully and precisely; agreement is not required, but evidence and transparency are. Never submit the same manuscript to multiple journals simultaneously unless the journals explicitly permit it. Assess journals critically. Verify the editorial board, peer-review process, indexing claims, fees, preservation, retraction policy, and publisher identity. A persuasive invitation is not evidence of quality. t: Developing as a Lifelong Academic Writer
x: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to apply the central concepts to a real assignment, research paper, thesis, or article in your own discipline. Reflect on growth as a writer and researcher. Identify transferable skills and future learning needs. Build a sustainable academic development plan. Learning objectives reflection scholarly identity transferable skill professional development research community Key terms Reflection is most useful when it leads to evidence-based action. Review drafts, feedback, research logs, and project outcomes to identify recurring strengths and problems. Ask not only what succeeded, but which conditions and decisions made success possible. Reflection as disciplined learning International students may negotiate multiple expectations about authority, participation, language, hierarchy, and collaboration. Scholarly identity does not require erasing prior linguistic or intellectual experience. It develops through responsible contribution, explicit communication, and increasingly independent judgment within and across communities. Scholarly identity across cultures Research and academic writing develop project management, information evaluation, data organization, analytical reasoning, communication, collaboration, ethical judgment, and persistence. Describe these skills through evidence: the task completed, the challenge addressed, the action taken, and the result achieved. Transferable skills Identify the next genre, method, language practice, software tool, or professional relationship that will extend your capacity. Set a concrete practice-and-feedback cycle. Degrees and publications are milestones, not the end of learning. Sustainable development balances ambition with integrity, wellbeing, and respect for collaborators. A continuing plan Academic development is cumulative. Maintain a portfolio containing proposals, ethics documents, search logs, data-management records, conference materials, reviewer responses, published outputs, and reflections on feedback. Record not only products but also decisions and skills that can transfer to a new project. Participate in seminars, laboratories, writing groups, and professional associations as sites of learning. In Korean academic settings, some norms may remain implicit: who speaks first, when drafts circulate, how disagreement is expressed, and how work is credited. Observe, but do not interpret silence as consent in matters of authorship, safety, ethics, workload, or assessment. Ask explicit, respectful questions. Set a yearly development plan across five domains: disciplinary knowledge, research design, academic English, collaboration, and public communication. Choose observable evidence for each goal—for example, a reproducible analysis script, an improved conference abstract, a bilingual terminology bank, or a documented authorship agreement. A sustainable identity is built through accountable practice, not through imitation of an imagined native speaker. Building a sustainable scholarly identity A doctoral student can compare successive versions of an interview protocol, a coding framework, a conference paper, and a journal response letter to identify how methodological judgment and scholarly voice have developed over time.
